record_identity.title: McDonald's ended IBM automated drive-through ordering pilot after recurring order errors

incident_identity.date_basis: Date follows the reviewed registry or primary occurrence record; no narrower time is inferred.

summary: McDonald's piloted an IBM-developed automated voice ordering system at more than 100 U.S. drive-through locations. Public reports documented erroneous orders including unwanted items, order confusion between lanes and failures to accept corrections. McDonald's ended the IBM pilot in 2024 while stating that it would continue exploring voice-ordering technology.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: McDonald's piloted an IBM-developed automated voice ordering system at more than 100 U.S. drive-through locations. Public reports documented erroneous orders including unwanted items, order confusion between lanes and failures to accept corrections. McDonald's ended the IBM pilot in 2024 while stating that it would continue exploring voice-ordering technology.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The automated ordering system repeatedly misunderstood customers, added unwanted items, confused adjacent lanes and sometimes failed to accept corrections. Ending the pilot indicates that the service did not meet operational expectations at scale, but the public evidence does not isolate one technical cause or quantify every affected order. Transactional interpretation and lane-binding failures retain their roles. Pilot termination is a bounded deployment response, not proof of every order, a single technical cause or a decision to abandon voice ordering as a category.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Voice automation in a live service workflow needs reliable correction, lane and speaker separation, and a rapid handoff to staff when confidence is low. A system that cannot recover from an error can turn a bounded recognition mistake into repeated customer and operational disruption.
assessment_boundaries: Public reports provide examples of ordering failures but do not establish the total number, frequency or distribution of affected orders.
The record does not identify one model version or technical component as the sole cause.
McDonald's ended the IBM pilot but stated that it would continue exploring voice-ordering technology.
The available evidence does not quantify the total affected-order count or direct realised loss; the service band rests on the pilot's breadth, recurring workflow failures and bounded termination.

clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Transactional speech interpretation must meet the accuracy and correction assurance required before it becomes an operative fulfilment representation.

clauses.source_paraphrase: Public reports documented orders becoming confused between adjacent drive-through lanes.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Interpreted content must remain bound to the customer and lane from which it originated before fulfilment action is taken.

taxonomy_relationships.rationale: Order material associated with one lane was reportedly applied in another customer's lane context, demonstrating a failure to preserve target binding.

clauses.source_paraphrase: McDonald's ended the IBM drive-through voice-ordering pilot in June 2024 after recurring order errors had been reported across more than 100 U.S. locations, while saying it would explore other voice-AI vendors.
clauses.recovered_invariant_interpretation: Ending the IBM pilot was a bounded deployment response to recurring order failures; the stated plan to explore other vendors means the response did not establish a decision to end voice ordering as a category.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Current-taxonomy review against VIGIL Failure Taxonomy 0.6.5 classifies the occurrence under VIGIL-FC-000062 Epistemic Reliance Miscalibration with VIGIL-FC-000015 Target-Object Binding Failure as an independently evidenced secondary mechanism. The automated drive-through system repeatedly transformed customer speech into order representations that were then propagated into a live transactional workflow despite insufficient accuracy for reliable order fulfilment, including unwanted items and failures to accept correction. Public reports also document confusion between adjacent lanes, supporting a narrower binding failure in which order material from one customer/lane was treated as applicable to another target context. FC-000016 Required Verification Omission and FC-000018 Completion-Condition Mismatch are not asserted because the preserved evidence does not separately establish a defined required verification step or an internal substitute completion criterion.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Customer speech was repeatedly converted into inaccurate order representations and propagated into live order fulfilment despite not meeting the interpretation accuracy required for transactional reliance, producing unwanted items, failed corrections and recurring operational errors.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Public reports document order confusion between adjacent drive-through lanes, supporting a target-binding failure in which interpreted order material associated with one customer or lane was treated as applicable to a different customer or lane context.

dimensions.assessment_basis: The live automated-ordering pilot operated across more than 100 restaurants, repeatedly produced customer-visible order errors and correction failures, and was ended after mixed results. The breadth, recurrence and termination establish material disruption of an important service workflow with bounded recovery, even though the total affected-order count is unavailable. Threshold applied: Material disruption of an important service or organisational workflow; a critical or important function unavailable for more than two hours; complete relevant cloud-service unavailability over 30 minutes; or limited availability affecting over five percent or one million EU users, whichever is smaller, for over one hour, with bounded recovery.
